title: HR Operations Excellence
tagline: Run the engine room of HR anywhere: clean records, accurate payroll, lawful policies, fair discipline and service people can trust.
description:
Every promise an organisation makes to its people is kept, or broken, by HR operations. The contract, the payslip, the leave balance, the fair hearing and the reply to a simple request all come from the engine room. This certification teaches that work at professional level for workplaces anywhere in the world: international standards first, then examples from many countries.

- **Lifecycle and records:** onboarding from offer to probation, worker classification, personnel files, HRIS data, data protection and the monthly headcount reconciliation.
- **Payroll:** gross-to-net calculation, allowances, deductions, pension funds, end-of-service gratuity, social security, overtime and income-tax withholding on salaries.
- **Law and policy:** ILO standards and the national, state and free-zone laws built on them, minimum wage, leave and working hours, handbooks and attendance management.
- **Employee relations:** grievances, show-cause notices, fair inquiries, proportionate penalties and harassment laws.
- **Service and control:** HR metrics with calculations, shared services and SLAs, compliance calendars and HR audits.

Every stage uses real cases, from Canada's Phoenix pay system to the UK Post Office scandal, and ends with a scored test; the final exam is tough, with calculations and realistic cases. Labour and tax rules differ by country and change often, so the course teaches how they work and reminds you to check the current law where you work before you apply a figure.
audience: HR officers and executives who run onboarding, records, leave, attendance and payroll inputs
Payroll and HRIS specialists who want a firmer grip on the law and controls behind the numbers
HR managers and business partners responsible for policies, employee relations and compliance in one or several countries
Plant, branch and line managers who handle attendance, grievances and discipline in their teams
Professionals moving into HR from finance, administration or operations
outcomes: Run a compliant onboarding, classify workers correctly and keep personnel files and HRIS data complete, accurate and protected
Calculate gross-to-net pay, overtime, unpaid-leave deductions, gratuity and mid-year tax withholding correctly
Explain how pension funds, end-of-service gratuity and state social security work, and who pays for what
Apply ILO standards and the law where people work, and write policies and leave rules that meet or beat it
Handle grievances and disciplinary cases with a fair show-cause and inquiry process that stands up to challenge
Calculate and interpret turnover, absenteeism, time-to-fill, cost-per-hire and SLA compliance
Design tiered HR service delivery and run audits with root-cause analysis and corrective action plans

quest.name: The Ninety-Day Audit at Tamarind Crest
quest.premise: Tamarind Crest Foods, a fast-growing snacks and dairy group run from Dubai, with plants in Nairobi, Monterrey and Faisalabad and a payroll centre in Kuala Lumpur, has just learned that its biggest global retail customer will audit the 1,200-person Nairobi plant in ninety days. Fail, and the export contract that feeds half the plant goes. You have joined as Group HR Operations Manager and find missing files, a payroll nobody fully trusts, an outdated handbook and a shop floor close to boiling. Five stages, ninety days: put the engine room in order.

cards.title: Day one at the gate
cards.setting: Tamarind Crest's Nairobi plant, Mombasa Road. 8:10 am. Delivery trucks queue at the gate while the morning shift clocks in.

lines.text: Stage one of your quest begins at the front gate. Ninety days from today, auditors from Tamarind Crest's biggest global retail customer will walk through it.
Welcome aboard. I flew in from Dubai to say this in person: the customer's audit decides the export contract, and our HR engine room has been running on WhatsApp and memory.
Example from this morning. Kevin, a packing operator, has worked here three weeks. No written contract, no social security registration, and his ID copy is a blurry photo on my phone.
He works well. Paperwork can wait. I need hands on the line, not files in a cupboard.

Joining by video from Kuala Lumpur, where we run payroll for all four sites. There's a bigger problem. The HRIS says 1,240 active employees in Nairobi. Last month we paid 1,262 people. I can't explain the 22.
Twenty-two people we pay but cannot see. Your first mission: rebuild the front gate so nobody walks in, or out, without HR knowing. Where do you start?

cards.title: One person, one journey, one record

scenes.heading: The employee lifecycle
scenes.narration: Every employee travels the same road: attracted, hired, onboarded, managed and developed, rewarded, and finally exited. HR operations is the machinery that keeps that road paved.

scenes.heading: Data follows the person
scenes.narration: At each stage something is recorded: an offer, a joining date, a promotion, a transfer, a leave balance, a last working day. If the record is wrong, everything built on it goes wrong too.

scenes.heading: Joiners, movers, leavers
scenes.narration: Operations teams often call this the joiner, mover, leaver process. A joiner needs a record, pay and access. A mover needs changes with the right effective date. A leaver needs pay stopped, access removed and a final settlement.

scenes.heading: Where ghosts are born
scenes.narration: When a leaver is not recorded before payroll cut-off, salary keeps flowing. When a joiner is paid outside the system, nobody can verify them. Both create the gap Mei found.

scenes.heading: The front gate
scenes.narration: So the front gate is not a guard post. It is a rule: nobody is paid, given access or put on a shift until their record is complete and approved.

cards.question: A candidate accepts an offer on the 3rd and joins on the 20th. Collecting her documents, checking her ID and right to work and creating her HRIS record during that gap is called what?
options: Induction
Probation review
Pre-boarding
Requisition approval
cards.explanation: Pre-boarding is the work between offer acceptance and day one, so the person arrives to a ready record, a letter and access. Induction is the welcome and orientation that starts on or after the first day.

cards.title: Onboarding: from offer to probation decision
cards.body:
Treat onboarding as three phases, each with a checklist and an owner.

- **Pre-boarding (offer to day one):** signed offer, documents, identity and **right-to-work** checks, education and reference checks with consent, medical fitness where the job needs it, HRIS record created and approved, pay and bank details, tax and social security registrations started.
- **Day one and induction:** written terms signed, handbook acknowledged, safety briefing, access, a buddy.
- **First 90 days:** objectives in week one, documented check-ins, and a probation decision **before** probation ends.

**Written terms are a legal duty in many places:** the UK requires a written statement from day one, EU law requires the core terms within about the first week, and South Asian standing-orders laws require them at appointment. Check the rule where you work. A contract promised "after probation" is a compliance gap, not a courtesy.

cards.title: Real case: H&M's fine for profiling staff (2020)
cards.body:
**What happened.** At H&M's service centre in Nuremberg, Germany, managers held "welcome back" talks after staff returned from holiday or sick leave, and recorded details of their private lives: illnesses, family problems, religious beliefs. The notes were stored where many managers could read them and were used to judge staff. They came to light in 2019 when a configuration error briefly made them visible across the company.

**Outcome.** In 2020 the Hamburg data protection authority fined H&M about **EUR 35 million** under the GDPR, one of the largest fines of its kind at the time. The company apologised and offered compensation to the staff affected.

**Lesson for HR operations:** return-to-work talks are useful, but record only what employment needs, restrict who can see it, and never build profiles of people's private lives.

cards.title: One master record, many users
cards.caption: The HRIS is the single source of truth. Payroll and finance read from it; they never keep a separate employee list.

items.detail: Joining, promotion, transfer, leave or exit is approved

items.label: Maker enters it
items.detail: HR officer records the change with its effective date

items.label: Checker approves
items.detail: A second person verifies against the source document

items.label: HRIS master updates
items.detail: Unique employee ID, audit trail logs who changed what

items.label: Payroll and access follow
items.detail: Pay, statutory returns and system access update from the master

cards.title: HRIS essentials that prevent expensive mistakes
cards.body:
- **Unique employee ID** linked to a national ID or passport number, so one person can never exist twice.
- **Master data:** the core facts (name, ID number, joining date, position, grade, pay, bank account) that other processes reuse.
- **Effective dating:** every change carries the date it takes effect, not the date it was typed. A raise approved in April but effective 1 March lets payroll calculate arrears.
- **Maker-checker:** one person enters, another approves. Nobody should both create an employee and approve their bank details.
- **Audit trail:** a log of who changed which field, when, from what to what.
- **Role-based access:** people see only what their job needs. A line manager sees team attendance, not colleagues' salaries or medical notes.
- **Monthly reconciliation:** active HRIS headcount must match the payroll register, and every difference is explained before payroll is approved.

One officer cannot add a fake employee and approve the bank account alone

pairs.left: Unique ID linked to national ID

cards.title: Real case: the Morrisons payroll leak (UK)
cards.body:
**What happened.** In 2014 a senior internal auditor at UK supermarket chain Morrisons, who held a grudge after an earlier disciplinary matter, was given payroll data to pass to the external auditors. He secretly copied the names, addresses, bank details and salaries of about **100,000 staff** and posted them online. He was convicted and jailed for eight years.

**Outcome.** Thousands of staff sued the company. In 2020 the UK Supreme Court ruled that Morrisons was not vicariously liable, because he was pursuing a personal vendetta rather than doing his job. Even so, the case took six years and cost the company heavily in time, money and trust.

**Lesson for HR operations:** the biggest threat to HR data often has legitimate access. Limit who can extract full payroll files, log every download, and review access rights regularly.

cards.title: Hunting the twenty-two
cards.setting: Payroll centre, Kuala Lumpur. Mei's screens show the Nairobi HRIS list beside last month's payroll register; Priya is on video from the plant.

lines.text: Matched by national ID number, not by name. Fifteen people left the plant in the last four months, but nobody sent their exit forms to HR before cut-off. They were still paid.
Four are new joiners Diego's supervisors added straight to payroll from a WhatsApp list. They work here, but they have no HRIS record.
And three are duplicates. Same person, ID number typed with one digit wrong, so the system created a second employee.
Fine, problem solved. Delete the twenty-two from payroll and move on. The auditors will never know.
Delete four real workers' pay? And never ask where fifteen salaries went? Think carefully. What do we actually do next?

cards.title: Closing the gap the right way
cards.situation: Your reconciliation explains all 22 differences: 15 leavers still paid for up to four months, 4 genuine joiners paid without HRIS records, and 3 duplicate records. Payroll for this month runs in six days. Diego wants all 22 simply deleted.

choices.text: Delete all 22 from payroll today so the numbers match before anyone asks
choices.outcome: The numbers match, but four real workers miss their pay and complain to Samuel, and nobody learns where fifteen leavers' salaries went. You fixed the report, not the problem.

choices.text: Stop the 15 leavers and 3 duplicates, onboard the 4 joiners properly, trace where the overpaid salaries went, start recovery, and fix the exit trigger so it cannot recur
choices.outcome: Leila nods. Each group gets the right treatment: real workers are protected, overpayments are traced (to the leavers' accounts or elsewhere) and recovered where possible, and the leaver process now starts in HRIS before cut-off.

choices.text: Stop the 15 leavers and 3 duplicates, and onboard the 4 joiners, but leave the past overpayments alone
choices.outcome: This month will be right, but four months of payments to leavers are unexplained. If any landed in someone else's account, that is possible fraud, and an auditor will ask what you did about it.

choices.text: Freeze the whole plant payroll until every file is perfect
choices.outcome: 1,200 people go unpaid over a records problem that affects 22. Wage-payment law and basic trust both suffer, and the shop floor erupts.

cards.front: Any manager can see any employee file. It's company property.
cards.back: Myth. Access should follow need-to-know. Managers see what their role requires; medical, harassment and salary details are restricted.

cards.front: Collect everything at joining, just in case.
cards.back: Myth. Collect only what you need for employment, pay, law and safety. Extra data is extra risk.

cards.front: Ex-employees can demand that every record is deleted immediately.
cards.back: Not quite. Keep what law, tax, pension and possible claims require for their retention periods; delete the rest on schedule and record why.

cards.front: Check references with the current employer without telling the candidate.
cards.back: Avoid it. Get the candidate's consent first; contacting a current employer unannounced can cost them their job.

cards.front: Does every country have a GDPR-style data protection law?
cards.back: Not every one. The EU's GDPR (2018) is the model many followed: Brazil, Kenya, Singapore, the UAE and India have their own laws, while elsewhere bills are still in draft. Check yours, and apply good practice anyway.

cards.front: A WhatsApp photo of an ID card is a fine record.
cards.back: No. Keep a clear, verified copy in the secure HR system, not on personal phones, and check the document itself, not just a picture of it.

cards.question: In the HRIS, Mei finds that the same payroll officer created a new employee and also approved that employee's bank account number. Which control has failed?
options: Effective dating
Maker-checker (segregation of duties)
Role-based access for line managers
Records retention schedule
cards.explanation: Maker-checker means one person enters a change and a different person approves it. When one person does both, a fictitious employee with a controlled bank account can be created without anyone noticing.

cards.title: Kevin's file, fixed in a day
cards.body:
Priya uses Kevin's case to pilot the new front gate.

- **Classification:** Kevin fills a permanent packing post and has worked three weeks, so he is a **probationer**, provisionally employed in a permanent vacancy. Other common classes: **permanent** (open-ended), **temporary or fixed-term** (work that will end, such as a seasonal rush), **cover or relief** (replacing a permanent worker who is temporarily away; called *badli* in South Asian law), **apprentice**, and **agency or contractor** workers supplied by a third party.
- **Written terms:** issued that day with classification, pay, hours, probation and notice. Kevin signs and keeps a copy.
- **Records:** ID and right to work verified; nominations signed; tax and social security registration submitted.
- **HRIS:** created by Priya, approved by Mei, joining date set to his real first day.

Diego loses Kevin for twenty minutes. The plant loses one audit finding.

cards.title: Five habits of a clean front gate
cards.body:
- **No record, no pay, no shift.** Payroll only pays approved HRIS records.
- **Exit before cut-off.** The leaver's last working day goes into HRIS the moment a resignation is accepted, not when clearance ends.
- **Match on ID numbers, not names.** Names repeat and get spelled several ways.
- **Real dates.** Backdating or forward-dating hides service and breaks leave and gratuity later.
- **Know the ghost signs:** several employees paid into one bank account, no attendance records, no verified ID.
- **Audit files monthly.** Sample ten and tick off each required document.

cards.question: The plant hires extra packers for three months to handle the year-end festive rush, with no permanent vacancy behind the posts. Under the classification taught here, which class fits best?
options: Cover (relief)
Probationer
Temporary (fixed-term)
Apprentice
cards.explanation: A temporary or fixed-term worker is engaged for work that is itself temporary and will end, like a seasonal rush. A cover worker replaces a permanent worker who is away, and a probationer fills a permanent vacancy; neither applies here.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Front Gate
items: HR operations runs the whole lifecycle: hire, onboard, manage, reward, relate and exit. Each stage creates data that others depend on.
Onboarding has three phases: pre-boarding, day one and induction, and the first 90 days ending in a timely probation decision.
Give written terms at or near the start, classify workers correctly, and keep a complete personnel file with restricted items stored separately.
The HRIS is the single source of truth: unique ID linked to national ID, effective dating, maker-checker, audit trail and role-based access.
Collect only the data employment needs, and limit and log who can extract it: the H&M and Morrisons cases show the cost of getting this wrong.
Reconcile HRIS headcount with payroll every month, explain every difference, and fix the process that created it.

cards.prompt: Think about your own organisation. If you compared last month's payroll register with your active headcount today, matched by ID number, would the numbers agree? Which part of your joiner or leaver process is most likely to create a gap?

quiz.question: Which phase of onboarding covers the period between a candidate accepting the offer and their first day at work?
options: Induction
Probation review
Pre-boarding
Workforce planning
quiz.explanation: Pre-boarding runs from offer acceptance to day one: documents, checks, HRIS record and registrations. Induction starts on or after the first day, and the probation review comes at the end of the first months.

quiz.question: A plant supervisor says new operators will receive written contracts only after they pass probation, "to save paperwork on people who may leave." What should HR do?
options: Agree, but make sure the offer letter mentions the probation period
Issue written terms of employment at joining
Agree, provided the operators are registered in the HRIS on their first day
Issue contracts after probation but backdate them to the joining date
quiz.explanation: Many laws require written terms at or near the start (from day one in the UK, within about a week for core terms in the EU, at appointment under South Asian standing orders), and it is good practice everywhere. An offer letter or an HRIS record does not replace them, and backdating creates a false record.

quiz.question: Which of these belongs in a restricted confidential file rather than the core personnel file?
options: A medical fitness report from the company doctor
The signed appointment letter stating pay and classification
Pension and benefit nomination forms
A verified copy of the employee's national ID
quiz.explanation: Medical information is sensitive and should be accessible only to those who need it, so it is stored separately. The appointment letter, nominations and ID copy are core employment records.

quiz.question: An increment approved in May is effective from 1 April. Which HRIS feature allows payroll to pay the April arrears automatically?
options: Maker-checker approval of the increment entry
Role-based access
Effective dating of the pay change
The audit trail
quiz.explanation: Effective dating records when a change takes effect, separately from when it was entered, so payroll can calculate the arrears for April. Maker-checker and the audit trail control and log the change but do not set its timing.

quiz.question: During a review you find that one HR officer can create a new employee record and also approve that employee's bank account details. What is the main risk?
options: Salary increments could be calculated from the wrong effective date each month
A fictitious employee could be paid into an account the officer controls
Line managers could see salary information they do not need
Personnel files could be kept longer than the retention schedule allows
quiz.explanation: Without maker-checker, one person can create a ghost employee and route pay to their own account. The other risks are real but are addressed by different controls.

quiz.question: The monthly reconciliation shows payroll paid 18 more people than the HRIS active list. Which explanation should be investigated first because it can mean money is leaving the company improperly?
options: Leavers who were still paid after their last working day
Employees whose job titles differ between the two systems
Employees whose leave balances were not yet updated
Joiners whose induction training is still pending
quiz.explanation: Leavers still on payroll mean salaries are being paid to people who no longer work there, which may also hide diversion of funds. Title mismatches, leave balances and training do not change who is paid.

quiz.question: A line manager asks HR for copies of all his team members' ID cards and home addresses "to send holiday greetings." What is the best response?
options: Share the ID copies but remove the home addresses
Share everything, since he manages these employees
Ask each employee to send the manager their ID copy directly
Decline, and offer to send the greetings through HR instead
quiz.explanation: Access follows need-to-know. Sending greetings does not require ID copies or addresses, and HR can achieve the purpose without disclosing personal data. Pushing employees to share it directly sidesteps the same principle.

quiz.question: In the worker classification taught in this stage, what is a probationer?
options: A worker provisionally employed to fill a permanent vacancy
A worker covering a permanent worker who is temporarily absent
A worker engaged for work that will finish within a limited time
A learner paid an allowance while being trained
quiz.explanation: A probationer fills a permanent vacancy on a provisional basis. Covering an absent permanent worker describes a cover (relief) worker, short-term work describes a temporary or fixed-term worker, and a paid learner is an apprentice.

quiz.question: Which change to the leaver process best prevents salaries being paid after people leave?
options: Remove the leaver from payroll once the final settlement has been calculated and paid
Ask supervisors to send HR a WhatsApp list of leavers at month-end
Record the last working day in HRIS as soon as the exit is confirmed, before payroll cut-off
Check the payroll register against the HRIS once a year at audit time
quiz.explanation: Pay stops reliably only when the exit date is in the master record before cut-off. Waiting for final settlement or a month-end list leaves gaps, and an annual check finds problems months too late.

quiz.question: A shortlisted candidate for a finance manager role asks you not to contact her current employer yet. What should you do?
options: Contact her current employer anyway, because references must come from the latest job
Drop her from the shortlist, since refusing a reference is a red flag
Skip all reference checks because she has refused one
Respect it: use other referees, verify documents and make any offer conditional
quiz.explanation: Reference checks need the candidate's consent, and an unannounced call can cost her the current job. Other referees, document verification and a conditional offer protect the company without that harm.

sessions.title: Payroll from Gross to Net: Allowances, Deductions, Funds and Tax
sessions.summary: Open the payroll vault: build gross pay from basic and allowances, take it to net through lawful deductions, calculate overtime and unpaid leave, understand pension funds, end-of-service gratuity and social security, withhold income tax on salaries correctly and run the controls that keep payroll trusted.
objectives: Calculate gross pay, employee deductions, net pay and the employer's cost of an employee
Calculate overtime, unpaid-leave deductions and gratuity from stated rules
Explain how pension funds, end-of-service gratuity and state social security work and who pays
Apply the annualised method of income-tax withholding on salaries, including mid-year changes
Run payroll controls: cut-off, variance review, maker-checker and segregation of duties

cards.title: The WhatsApp storm
cards.setting: Payroll centre, Kuala Lumpur. Mei's phone buzzes non-stop: the Nairobi plant workers' WhatsApp group has 340 unread messages.

lines.text: Stage two. The twenty-two are fixed, but closing them opened the payroll vault, and not everything inside is pretty.
Six months of night overtime, and the rate on the payslip is the same as a normal hour. Our collective agreement says double. The boys are talking about a go-slow.
He's right, I checked. Someone set the Nairobi overtime factor to 1 instead of 2 when we moved to the new payroll system. And forty staff in Monterrey have pension taken on gross instead of basic.
And the managers at our Faisalabad plant are asking why their tax jumped in January after their raises. Nobody explained anything.
A payroll nobody understands is a payroll nobody trusts. The auditors will interview workers about their pay.
Your mission: learn this vault from gross to net, fix what is wrong, and be able to explain any payslip to anyone, in any of our countries. Ready?

cards.title: The journey of a dollar from gross to net

scenes.heading: Basic salary first
scenes.narration: Pay starts with basic salary. It matters more than its size suggests, because pension contributions, end-of-service gratuity and often overtime are calculated from it.

scenes.heading: Allowances build gross
scenes.narration: Housing, transport and other allowances are added to basic. Basic plus allowances, plus any overtime or arrears, gives gross pay for the month.

scenes.heading: Deductions take it to net
scenes.narration: From gross, payroll subtracts income tax withheld, the employee's pension and social security contributions, loan instalments and any lawful recoveries. What remains is net pay, the amount in the bank.

scenes.heading: The employer pays more
scenes.narration: On top of gross, the employer pays its own pension and social security contributions, and sets aside a provision for end-of-service gratuity where law or policy requires one. Together that is the cost to company.

scenes.heading: Money owed to others
scenes.narration: Tax withheld and statutory contributions are not the company's money. They must be deposited on time, with returns filed, or the employer faces penalties.

cards.title: The monthly payroll cycle
cards.caption: Most countries set a legal deadline for paying wages, and ILO Convention 95 (1949) requires wages to be paid regularly. Check the deadline where you work.

cards.question: Under a typical scheme design, which of these is normally calculated as a percentage of basic salary rather than gross pay?
options: Net pay
Income tax withheld
The unpaid-leave deduction under a gross-based policy
The pension or provident fund contribution
cards.explanation: Pension and provident fund rules usually set contributions as a percentage of basic (or 'pensionable') salary. That is why Mei's finding of pension taken on gross for forty Monterrey staff is an error. Income tax is worked out on taxable salary, not just basic.

cards.title: Building gross and getting to net
cards.body:
Pay structures differ by country and company. An illustrative structure:

| | USD |
|---|---|
| Basic | 4,000 |
| Housing allowance (25% of basic) | 1,000 |
| Transport allowance (flat) | 200 |
| **Gross** | **5,200** |
| Pension, employee 5% of basic | −200 |
| Social security, employee (illustrative 2% of gross) | −104 |
| Income tax withheld (illustrative) | −600 |
| Loan instalment | −150 |
| **Net** | **4,146** |

Tax, pension and social security rates are set by each country's law and scheme rules, and they change often. Use the current figures for the country where the employee works.

cards.title: One payslip, four numbers

Overtime for extra hours worked
Arrears of an increment

cards.title: Pensions, gratuity and social security
cards.body:
- **Pension or provident fund:** employee and employer each pay a set % of basic or pensionable pay into a scheme held **separately from the company**, by trustees or a state body. Examples: Singapore's CPF, Malaysia's EPF, India's EPF, UK workplace pensions under auto-enrolment. Approved schemes usually get tax advantages within limits.
- **End-of-service gratuity:** a lump sum for service, set by law or policy. UAE private-sector law: **21 days' basic pay for each of the first five years**, then 30 days for each later year. India: 15 days' wages per completed year, after five years' service. Pakistan's standing orders: 30 days' wages per completed year. In India and Pakistan a final part-year counts only if it is **more than six months**.
- **State social security:** contributions set by law for pensions, health or injury cover, such as US Social Security, UK National Insurance or Kenya's NSSF. Rates, ceilings and who pays differ.

Check the current rules where the employee works.

cards.front: Is pension or provident fund money the company's money?
cards.back: No. It belongs to the members and sits in a trust or state scheme, separate from the company's own accounts.

cards.front: 7 years 8 months' service, last basic USD 3,000 a month. Gratuity at 30 days' basic per completed year?
cards.back: 30 days' basic is one month's basic. The 8 months exceed six, so count 8 years: 8 × 3,000 = USD 24,000.
Four months does not exceed six, so 7 years: 7 × 3,000 = USD 21,000.

cards.front: UAE rule: 3 years' service, basic AED 6,000 a month, daily rate basic ÷ 30. Gratuity?
cards.back: 21 days for each of the first five years. Daily basic = 6,000 ÷ 30 = 200. 3 × 21 × 200 = AED 12,600.
It depends on the country. In the US and the UK both employer and employee contribute; some schemes are funded by the employer alone. Check the current law.
Funded: money set aside in an approved fund, often valued by an actuary. Unfunded: a provision in the company's books, paid from its own cash on exit.

cards.title: Double means double
cards.setting: Plant HR office, Nairobi. Samuel sits across from you with a folder of payslips. Priya has the attendance register open; Mei is on the video call.

lines.text: Our collective agreement says plant overtime is paid at twice the ordinary rate. Ours were paid one times for six months.
Fifty workers, about twenty overtime hours each a month, ordinary rate about KES 180 an hour. They were paid 180 instead of 360 for every overtime hour.
Can we fix it from next month and call it even? Arrears for six months will blow my plant budget.
If you only fix it from next month, the boys will take that as an insult. They worked those hours.
Run the numbers. Then decide what a fair, lawful fix looks like before Samuel's WhatsApp group decides for us.

cards.title: Fixing the overtime underpayment
cards.situation: The shortfall is KES 180 for each overtime hour: 50 workers × 20 hours × 6 months × KES 180 = KES 1,080,000. Diego wants to correct the rate from next month only. Samuel is waiting for an answer.

choices.text: Correct the rate from next month and quietly pay arrears only to workers who complain
choices.outcome: Word spreads within a day. Paying only those who complain is unfair, keeps the underpayment for everyone else, and turns into a grievance and an audit finding.

choices.text: Correct the rate and pay arrears in six instalments, explained to Samuel and the workers in advance
choices.outcome: It respects the debt and protects the budget, and Samuel may accept it. But wages already earned are owed now, and spreading them out without agreement risks a breach of wage-payment law.

choices.text: Correct the rate in the system, pay the full KES 1,080,000 in arrears with a clear explanation on payslips, and add a rate check to the monthly variance review
choices.outcome: Samuel takes the news to the floor and the go-slow talk stops. The law is met, workers see the error owned and repaid, and the control makes a repeat unlikely.

choices.text: Correct the rate from next month only, since the error was a system fault and not deliberate
choices.outcome: Intent does not reduce the debt. Workers were underpaid for hours they worked, and a labour inspector or auditor will treat it as unpaid wages.

cards.title: Real case: Queensland Health's payroll failure (2010)
cards.body:
**What happened.** In March 2010 the health department of Queensland, Australia, moved pay for tens of thousands of staff onto a new payroll system. Complex award rules and rosters had not been properly configured or tested. From the first pay runs, nurses and other staff were underpaid, overpaid or not paid at all.

**Outcome.** A Commission of Inquiry reported in 2013 that the project had been badly governed and tested, and put the total cost of the failure at about **AUD 1.2 billion**. Recovering overpayments from staff took years.

**Lesson for HR operations:** test every pay rule (overtime factors, allowances, shift premiums) against real cases before go-live, and run old and new systems side by side until the results match. One wrong factor, like the overtime rate in Nairobi, repeats every month until someone checks.

cards.title: Why the Faisalabad managers' tax jumped
cards.body:
Employers withhold income tax from salary each month. Some countries, such as India and Pakistan, use an **annualised method**:

1. **Project** taxable salary for the whole tax year.
2. **Apply** that year's rates. Budgets change them, normally from the start of the tax year.
3. **Spread** the annual tax: annual tax ÷ 12.
4. **When pay changes**, recalculate: (new projected annual tax − tax already deducted) ÷ remaining months.

In Pakistan the tax year runs July to June. A Faisalabad manager's projected annual tax was PKR 120,000, so 10,000 a month: 60,000 by December. A January raise lifts it to 150,000 (illustrative). For the 6 remaining months: (150,000 − 60,000) ÷ 6 = **15,000 a month**. A year's extra tax falls into six months, so take-home rises less than the raise. Explain it in the increment letter.

Tax years differ: 1 January in the US and Kenya, 6 April in the UK, 1 April in India, 1 July in Pakistan.

cards.question: Your payroll uses the annualised method and a tax year from April to March. From April to June an employee had USD 600 a month withheld. A raise effective July lifts her projected annual tax to USD 11,700. What should be withheld each month from July to March?
options: USD 975
USD 600
cards.explanation: Tax already deducted is 3 × 600 = 1,800. Remaining months July to March = 9. (11,700 − 1,800) ÷ 9 = 1,100. Dividing 11,700 by 12 ignores what was already deducted, and dividing it by 9 ignores the 1,800 already paid.

Clearance from departments: assets returned, loans confirmed

cards.question: Which of these is part of the company's cost of employing someone but never appears as a deduction on that employee's payslip?
options: The employee's pension contribution
Income tax withheld on salary
The employer's social security contribution
A staff loan instalment
cards.explanation: The employer's social security contribution is paid on top of gross, so it adds to cost to company without reducing net pay. The employee's pension share, tax and loan instalments are all deducted from gross.

cards.title: Controls that keep the vault locked
cards.body:
- **Variance review:** compare every department's total and headcount with last month. Any unexplained jump stops approval.
- **Segregation of duties:** the person who changes bank details or pay rates never releases the bank file.
- **Control totals:** the bank file total must equal the approved payroll net total.
- **Rate checks:** test overtime factors, pension % and allowance % after every system change.
- **Hourly rate:** convert the monthly ordinary wage with the divisor your policy states, such as 26 days × 8 hours.
- **Unpaid leave:** apply the divisor your policy states (for example gross ÷ 30 per day) consistently.
- **Confidential payslips:** each employee sees only their own.

cards.title: Real case: Canada's Phoenix pay system (2016)
cards.body:
**What happened.** In 2016 the Government of Canada moved pay for its federal public servants onto a new system called Phoenix, while cutting many of the experienced pay advisers who used to catch and fix errors. Within months, a large share of employees were underpaid, overpaid or not paid, and the backlog of pay cases grew into the hundreds of thousands.

**Outcome.** In 2018 the Auditor General of Canada called the project an incomprehensible failure of project management and oversight. Fixing it, and planning a replacement, has cost the government billions of dollars.

**Lesson for HR operations:** payroll controls need people as well as software. Keep expert reviewers, run variance checks every cycle, and do not remove the old safety net until the new one is proven.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Payroll Vault
items: Gross = basic + allowances + overtime and arrears; net = gross − tax, employee pension and social security, loans and other lawful deductions.
Cost to company adds the employer's pension and social security contributions and any gratuity provision on top of gross.
Overtime is paid at the premium the law or agreement sets; underpaid overtime is unpaid wages and must be repaid in full.
Gratuity follows the rule in law or policy, such as 30 days' basic per completed year or the UAE's 21 days for each of the first five years. Apply part-year rules exactly.
Annualised tax: project the year, apply current rates, and on any change spread (annual tax − tax deducted) over the remaining months.
Test every pay rule after a system change, and keep variance review, maker-checker and control totals: Queensland Health and Phoenix show the cost of skipping them.

cards.prompt: Pick your own last payslip. Can you trace every line from basic to net, and name which contributions your employer pays on top that never appear as deductions? Which line would you struggle to explain to a worker on the shop floor?

quiz.question: What does gross pay mean on a monthly payslip?
options: Basic salary before allowances are added
The amount actually paid into the employee's bank account
Total earnings for the month before any deductions
Total earnings plus the employer's contributions
quiz.explanation: Gross is all earnings (basic, allowances, overtime, arrears) before deductions. The bank amount is net pay, and earnings plus employer contributions is closer to cost to company.

quiz.question: An officer's basic salary is USD 3,000. Company policy sets the housing allowance at 25% of basic and the transport allowance at 10% of basic. What is her gross monthly pay?
quiz.explanation: Housing = 750 and transport = 300, so gross = 3,000 + 750 + 300 = 4,050. USD 3,750 leaves out transport; USD 3,300 leaves out housing.

quiz.question: For the same officer (basic USD 3,000, gross USD 4,050), the pension rules set the employee contribution at 5% of basic. What should be deducted each month?
options: USD 300
USD 150
USD 120
quiz.explanation: 5% of basic 3,000 = 150. USD 202.50 is 5% of gross, the exact mistake Mei found in Monterrey; USD 300 adds the employer's matching share, which is not deducted from the employee.

quiz.question: Which statement about state social security contributions is most accurate?
options: Rates, ceilings and who pays are set by each country's law, so payroll applies the current local rules
Employer and employee always pay equal shares, whatever the country
It is a voluntary scheme that employees may join if they choose
It is paid once a year from company profits into a workers' fund
quiz.explanation: Social security is statutory and differs by country: in the US and the UK both sides contribute, while some schemes are funded by the employer alone. Payroll must apply the current local rates and ceilings.

quiz.question: A machine operator's ordinary wage works out to USD 20 per hour. He worked 12 overtime hours this month, and his collective agreement pays overtime at twice the ordinary rate. What is his overtime pay?
options: USD 240
USD 360
USD 960
USD 480
quiz.explanation: Overtime rate = 2 × 20 = 40; 12 × 40 = 480. USD 240 is single rate (the Nairobi error), USD 360 is time-and-a-half and USD 960 doubles the rate twice.

quiz.question: A worker leaves after 5 years and 7 months. Her last-drawn basic was USD 2,500 a month and the policy pays gratuity of 30 days' basic per completed year, counting a final part-year of more than six months as a year. What is her gratuity?
quiz.explanation: Seven months is more than six, so count 6 years: 6 × 2,500 = 15,000. USD 12,500 ignores the part-year; USD 13,958 pro-rates it, which the rule does not do.

quiz.question: Your payroll uses the annualised method with a tax year from April to March. An employee had USD 800 withheld each month from April to July (USD 3,200 in total). From August a raise lifts his projected annual tax to USD 13,200. What should be withheld each month from August to March?
options: USD 800
quiz.explanation: (13,200 − 3,200) ÷ 8 remaining months = 1,250. USD 1,100 is 13,200 ÷ 12, which ignores the lower deductions already made; USD 1,650 divides the full annual tax by 8.

quiz.question: A policy deducts unpaid leave at gross ÷ 30 per day. An officer on USD 3,000 gross took 2 days of leave without pay. What is the deduction?
options: USD 100
USD 200
USD 194
USD 231
quiz.explanation: 3,000 ÷ 30 = 100 per day; 2 days = 200. USD 194 uses a 31-day divisor and USD 231 uses 26 days. Whichever divisor the policy states must be applied consistently.

quiz.question: Under the UAE rule taught here (21 days' basic pay for each of the first five years), an employee leaves after exactly 4 years on a basic salary of AED 9,000 a month. Using a daily rate of basic ÷ 30, what is the gratuity?
quiz.explanation: Daily basic = 9,000 ÷ 30 = 300. 4 years × 21 days × 300 = 25,200. AED 36,000 applies 30 days a year, AED 29,077 uses a 26-day divisor instead of the stated 30, and AED 6,300 counts only one year.

quiz.question: In the variance review, the warehouse department's payroll is 18% higher than last month with no change in headcount and no increments due. What should the payroll lead do?
options: Approve it, since headcount has not changed and the totals look broadly reasonable
Approve, and look into the difference after salaries are paid
Hold approval of that department until the increase is explained and evidenced
Reduce the department's total by 18% to match last month
quiz.explanation: An unexplained jump could be an overtime error, a wrong rate or fraud. Approving first means paying out money that may be wrong; cutting the total blindly could underpay people who earned the overtime.

sessions.title: Employment Law, Policies, Attendance and Leave
sessions.summary: Find your way through employment law, from the ILO's international standards to the national, state and free-zone laws that apply where people work: minimum wage, working hours, leave and contract labour. Then turn the law into a handbook people actually follow, and manage attendance and leave fairly and consistently.
objectives: Explain how ILO standards, national law and state, provincial or free-zone law fit together, and which law applies where
Apply the core baselines on minimum wage, working hours, overtime and leave, and know when to check local law
Place company policy correctly in the hierarchy of law, agreements, contracts and procedures
Write, launch and maintain policies and a handbook that employees understand and acknowledge
Manage attendance and leave consistently, including calculating the Bradford factor

cards.title: The 2014 handbook
cards.setting: Plant HR office, Nairobi. A dusty binder titled 'Employee Handbook 2014' sits open on Priya's desk. Samuel has brought two loaders with him.

lines.text: Stage three. Payroll is cleaner, but the auditors will also test what Tamarind Crest promises its people, and whether those promises meet the law.
These two are loaders from the labour contractor. KES 14,500 a month for full shifts, no social security card. Everyone knows that is below the minimum wage for their grade.
And the handbook says sick leave is 'at the manager's discretion'. Supervisors refuse it whenever production is busy.
The loaders are the contractor's people, not ours. And my old plant in Monterrey has a modern handbook. Copy it, change the logo, done.
A handbook written for Mexican law, used in a Kenyan plant? And contract workers below minimum wage inside our gate? Both would sink the audit.
Your mission at the Rulebook Archive: learn which rules apply to us, and rebuild a handbook that meets them. Where does labour law even come from?

scenes.heading: The international floor
scenes.narration: The International Labour Organization, founded in 1919, sets conventions on hours, wages, leave, safety and harassment. Countries that ratify a convention commit to bring their own law into line with it.

scenes.heading: National law
scenes.narration: Each country turns those standards into its own labour code, minimum wages and enforcement. The details vary a lot: overtime, leave and notice rules differ from one country to the next.

scenes.heading: Layers inside a country
scenes.narration: In federal countries, states or provinces add their own laws. US states can set minimum wages above the federal one, and since Pakistan's 18th Amendment in 2010, labour there is largely a provincial subject.

scenes.heading: Zones with their own rules
scenes.narration: Some business zones have their own employment law. In Dubai, employers in the Dubai International Financial Centre, the DIFC, follow the DIFC's own employment law rather than the UAE's federal labour law.

scenes.heading: So, which law?
scenes.narration: Ask where the person actually works, what kind of establishment it is, how many workers it has, and whether the person is a worker or a manager. The answers tell you which rules apply.

scenes.heading: Your safe habit
scenes.narration: Never copy a policy from another country, state or company. Check the current law where people work, and get legal review before you publish anything.

cards.title: Landmarks in the global rulebook
cards.caption: International standards set the floor. Countries ratify and legislate at their own pace, so always check the law in force where you work.

items.label: ILO founded; hours convention
items.detail: Convention 1: 8-hour day, 48-hour week, overtime at 1.25 times or more

items.label: Protection of wages
items.detail: Convention 95: regular payment of wages and limits on deductions

items.label: Minimum wages and paid holidays
items.detail: Conventions 131 and 132: minimum wage fixing; at least 3 weeks' paid leave

items.label: Fundamental rights declaration
items.detail: Freedom of association; no forced labour, child labour or discrimination

items.label: Maternity protection
items.detail: Convention 183: at least 14 weeks of maternity leave

items.label: EU Working Time Directive
items.detail: 48-hour average week, daily rest, 4 weeks' paid annual leave

items.label: Violence and harassment convention
items.detail: Convention 190: first global treaty on harassment at work

items.label: Safety becomes a fundamental right
items.detail: A safe and healthy working environment added to the ILO's fundamental principles

cards.question: Where should Tamarind Crest look first for the leave and working-hours rules that apply to its Nairobi plant?
options: Mexico's labour law, because the plant manager's handbook came from Monterrey
ILO conventions alone, because they replace national law
Kenya's labour laws, the law of the country where the plant operates
The retail customer's code of conduct, which replaces local law
cards.explanation: Labour law applies where the work is done. ILO conventions guide national law, but employers apply the national (and any local) law in force. A customer's code adds requirements but never replaces the law.

cards.title: The hierarchy of rules
cards.caption: A lower level may give more than a higher one, never less. A collective agreement binds the workers it covers until it is lawfully renegotiated.

items.label: Constitution and statutes
items.detail: Minimum wage, hours, leave, safety, discipline, harassment law

items.label: Collective agreements and awards
items.detail: Agreed terms for covered workers, often above the legal minimum

items.label: Employment contract
items.detail: Individual terms in the appointment letter

items.label: Company policy
items.detail: Rules the company sets for everyone, within the levels above

items.label: Procedures and guidelines
items.detail: How to apply the policy in practice

cards.title: The core rules you apply every week
cards.body:
International standards set the floor; national law sets the numbers you apply. **Check the current law where people work** before relying on any figure.

- **Minimum wage:** set nationally, by region or by sector. It covers contract and agency workers on your premises too.
- **Hours and overtime:** daily and weekly limits, rest breaks and a weekly rest day. Hours beyond the limit are overtime, paid at the premium the law or agreement sets.
- **Leave:** annual, sick, maternity and public holidays, each with its own qualifying rules.
- **Who is covered:** worker-protection rules focus on **workers**; managers' terms come mainly from their contracts and company policy. A collective agreement covers the workers it was negotiated for.
- **Records:** keep hours, overtime and leave records. Inspectors and auditors ask for them first.

Policy may give more than the law, never less.

cards.title: Same rule, different places
cards.caption: Examples only. Laws change, and states, provinces and collective agreements often add more. Check the current rule where you work.

items.label: Working hours
items.left: ILO C1: 8 a day, 48 a week
items.right: EU: 48-hour average incl. overtime; Pakistan factories: 9 a day, 48 a week

items.label: Overtime pay
items.right: US: 1.5 times after 40 hours a week; Pakistan factories: twice the ordinary rate

items.label: Annual leave
items.right: EU: 4 weeks; UK: 5.6 weeks; US: no federal right to paid leave

items.label: Maternity leave
items.right: Ranges widely; many countries go well beyond the floor

items.label: Minimum wage
items.right: National, regional or sector rates; US states may set more than the federal rate

Overtime paid at the rate the law and the collective agreement set
A regional manager's notice period set in his contract

cards.title: Real case: Uber drivers are workers (UK, 2021)
cards.body:
**What happened.** Uber treated its UK drivers as self-employed partners, so they received no minimum wage or paid holiday. Two drivers, Yaseen Aslam and James Farrar, brought a claim in 2016 arguing that they were in fact workers.

**Outcome.** In February 2021 the UK Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the drivers were **workers**, entitled to the minimum wage and paid holiday. The court looked at the reality of the relationship: Uber set fares and contract terms, controlled how drivers worked and could penalise them. The labels in Uber's own contracts did not decide it. Uber later said it would pay its UK drivers at least the minimum wage, holiday pay and pension contributions.

**Lesson for HR operations:** a worker's status depends on how the work is really done, not on what the contract calls it. Review contractor and agency arrangements against that test.

cards.title: The contractor's people
cards.setting: Loading bay, Nairobi plant, 6 pm. Forty contract loaders finish the day shift. The contractor, Joseph, waits by his motorbike.

lines.text: Forty loaders, KES 14,500 each for a full month. If the minimum for their grade is KES 17,000, that is a 2,500 shortfall per person, every month.
Joseph's contract says he is responsible for his workers. Not our problem.
They load our trucks, inside our gate, in our uniforms. The auditors will not care whose payroll they sit on.
Samuel is right about the risk. In many countries a principal employer that lets a contractor underpay can be pulled into the liability, and our customer will treat it as our failure.
So, what do we do with Joseph tomorrow morning?

cards.title: Fixing contract labour
cards.situation: Forty contract loaders have been paid KES 14,500 a month for three months against a minimum wage for their grade of KES 17,000 (assumed for this exercise). None is registered for social security. The customer's audit is in sixty days.

choices.text: Tell Joseph to pay the minimum wage from next month and leave the past alone
choices.outcome: The future is fixed, but KES 300,000 of underpayment (40 × 2,500 × 3) stays unpaid and the workers stay unregistered. Auditors who interview the loaders will find it.

choices.text: Require Joseph to pay arrears and the full minimum wage, register the workers, and prove it monthly with bank-paid salary records; write these duties into his contract
choices.outcome: The workers are paid what the law requires, the proof sits in your file, and the contract now lets you act if Joseph slips. This is how a principal employer manages contract labour.

choices.text: Accept Joseph's word that the workers are paid correctly and file his letter
choices.outcome: A letter is not evidence. Samuel already knows the real figure, and so will the auditors when they speak to the loaders.

choices.text: Terminate Joseph's contract at once and let the loaders go with him
choices.outcome: Forty people lose their jobs and their arrears with no fix. The underpayment that happened inside your gate is still your reputational problem, and the trucks stop.

cards.title: Real case: boohoo's Leicester suppliers (UK, 2020)
cards.body:
**What happened.** In 2020 UK media reported that garment workers in some Leicester factories making clothes for the online retailer boohoo were paid well below the national minimum wage and worked in poor conditions.

**Outcome.** The company commissioned an independent review by a senior barrister, Alison Levitt QC. Her report, published in September 2020, found the reports about pay and conditions substantially true and boohoo's monitoring of its supply chain inadequate, though it did not find that the company had deliberately profited from the abuses. Boohoo accepted the findings, cut ties with a number of suppliers and committed to reforms.

**Lesson for HR operations:** you cannot outsource responsibility for people who work for you through someone else. Verify contractors' pay with evidence, not letters.

cards.title: Policies that people actually follow
cards.body:
- **Policy:** what the company commits to and requires. *"Employees receive 20 days of annual leave."*
- **Procedure:** how it is done, step by step. *"Apply in the HRIS at least three days ahead; the supervisor approves within two days."*
- **Guideline:** advice that allows judgement. *"Managers are encouraged to spread leave across the year."*

A good handbook:
- Meets or beats the law of the country, state or zone where people work.
- Matches the collective agreement for covered workers.
- Is written plainly, with **versions in the languages people read**, such as Swahili in Nairobi or Spanish in Monterrey.
- Is **acknowledged** by each employee (signature or HRIS click) and explained in training.
- Has an owner, a version number and an **annual review date**.

A policy nobody has seen cannot be fairly enforced.

cards.title: Launching the new handbook
cards.prompt: Arrange the policy lifecycle steps for the plant's new handbook.
steps: Identify gaps against current local law and the collective agreement
Draft the policies in plain language
Legal review and consultation, including the union where required
Approve through the authority set by the board
Translate, communicate and train supervisors
Collect each employee's acknowledgment
Monitor use and review at least yearly

cards.back: Leave earned over time, for example a share of the annual entitlement each month, so balances grow as service grows.
Unused leave moved to the next year, within limits the law or policy sets.
Paying unused leave in cash, often at exit, at the rate and limit the policy states.
Absence approved but unpaid, deducted using the policy's divisor, such as gross ÷ 30 per day.
Absence without approval or notice. Repeated or prolonged absence can become a disciplinary matter.
A short, supportive conversation after each absence that checks wellbeing, reasons and any pattern.

cards.title: The Bradford factor: why short spells hurt more
cards.caption: Bradford factor = S² × D, where S is the number of separate absence spells and D the total days absent in the period. It flags frequent short absences. Exclude approved planned leave, maternity leave and workplace injuries.

items.label: Worker A: 1 spell, 10 days
items.detail: 1² × 10. One long illness, low disruption score

items.label: Worker B: 5 spells, 10 days
items.detail: 5² × 10. Same days, far more disruption

items.label: Worker C: 10 spells, 10 days
items.detail: 10² × 10. A pattern worth a supportive conversation

cards.question: Over six months a worker had 4 separate absence spells totalling 5 days. What is his Bradford factor?
cards.explanation: S² × D = 4² × 5 = 16 × 5 = 80. 20 is S × D, which ignores the squaring that makes frequent spells weigh more; 100 is 5² × 4, with S and D swapped.

cards.title: Which ILO convention?
cards.prompt: Match each ILO convention to the topic it covers.

pairs.right: Hours of work in industry, with overtime paid at a premium
Protection of wages, including limits on deductions
Paid annual leave of at least three working weeks

cards.body:
Priya and you compare the 2014 handbook with current Kenyan law and the plant's collective agreement.

- **Sick leave:** "at manager's discretion" is replaced with the legal entitlement (or better), plus a rule that a medical certificate is needed for longer absences. Supervisors can no longer refuse it for production reasons.
- **Annual leave:** the collective agreement gives plant workers more days than the legal minimum the draft quoted, so the draft is corrected; the agreement prevails for covered workers.
- **Contract labour:** a new section requires contractors to pay at least the minimum wage, register workers and provide monthly proof.
- **Language:** English and Swahili versions; supervisors trained in two short sessions.
- **Acknowledgment:** each worker signs; office staff click in the HRIS.

Diego's Monterrey handbook is politely returned. It cited Mexican law, which does not govern a plant in Kenya.

cards.title: Fair attendance management
cards.body:
- **Link biometric data to rosters** in the HRIS so lateness and absence are measured against the actual shift.
- **Hold a return-to-work talk after every absence.** Most patterns improve once someone notices.
- **Use triggers, not instincts:** for example, a Bradford score or a number of spells that leads to a formal review.
- **Be consistent:** the same trigger for the favourite operator and the difficult one.
- **Never penalise protected absence:** approved statutory leave, maternity leave, or injury at work.
- **Look for causes:** Monday absences on one line may point to a supervisor, transport or a second job.

cards.question: An employee in an EU country asks what minimum paid annual leave EU law guarantees. What does the Working Time Directive set?
options: Three working weeks
Four weeks
5.6 weeks
Two weeks
cards.explanation: The EU Working Time Directive guarantees at least four weeks of paid annual leave. Three working weeks is the ILO Convention 132 floor, and 5.6 weeks is the UK's own statutory figure, which goes beyond the EU minimum.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Rulebook Archive
items: ILO conventions set the international floor; national, state, provincial or free-zone law sets the rules you apply. Check the law where the person works.
Know the baselines and their local versions: 8 hours a day and 48 a week (ILO), overtime at 1.25 times or more, at least 3 weeks' paid leave, at least 14 weeks' maternity leave.
Minimum wages apply to contract workers inside your gate. A principal employer must verify contractor compliance, as Uber and boohoo learned.
Law and collective agreements sit above contracts and policies. Policies can give more, never less.
Policies need plain language, versions in the languages people read, acknowledgment, training, an owner and annual review.
Manage attendance with consistent triggers such as the Bradford factor (S² × D) and supportive return-to-work talks.

cards.prompt: Open your organisation's handbook. Find one rule that is vague (like 'at the manager's discretion'), one that may not match the current law where you work, and one that employees have probably never read. What would you change first?

quiz.question: Since Pakistan's 18th Amendment in 2010, labour there has been largely a provincial subject. What is the general lesson for HR in any country where states or provinces make labour law?
options: Only national law matters, so state or provincial rules can be ignored
Every site may follow the law of the state where head office sits
Check the law of the state or province where people actually work
The company may choose whichever state's law suits it best
quiz.explanation: Where states or provinces make labour law, the rules of the place where the work is done apply to that work. Head-office location or company preference does not change which law applies.

quiz.question: A labour contractor supplies daily-wage loaders to your Nairobi plant. Does a minimum wage apply to them?
options: No, because they are not the plant's own employees
Only the minimum wage of the contractor's home town
No; the contractor may set any wage the workers agree to in writing
Yes: the minimum wage where they work applies, even though the contractor pays them
quiz.explanation: Minimum wage rules cover workers employed through contractors at the place where they work. A worker's written agreement cannot waive the statutory minimum, and the contractor's home town does not decide the rate.

quiz.question: A company policy grants fewer days of a type of leave than the applicable law requires. What is the legal position?
options: The legal entitlement applies; policy cannot give less than the law
The policy applies, because every employee acknowledged it in writing
The policy applies until the next annual review
Each manager decides which applies to his team
quiz.explanation: Statutes sit at the top of the hierarchy. A policy can improve on the law but cannot reduce statutory rights, even with an employee's signature.

quiz.question: During a walk-through you learn that a security contractor pays its guards at your site below the notified minimum wage. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Take no action, because the guards are employed by the contractor
Make the contractor pay the minimum and arrears, with monthly proof under the contract
Ask the guards to sign letters confirming they are fully satisfied with their pay and conditions
Replace the guards with a cheaper contractor before anyone notices
quiz.explanation: A principal employer should make contractors comply and verify it, because underpayment at its site creates legal and reputational risk. Satisfaction letters do not cure an unlawful wage, and switching contractors fixes nothing.

quiz.question: Which of these statements is a procedure rather than a policy?
options: Apply for annual leave in the HRIS at least three working days ahead
Employees are entitled to 20 days of annual leave a year
The company does not tolerate harassment of any kind
Overtime is paid at twice the ordinary rate for all plant workers on every shift
quiz.explanation: A procedure says how something is done, such as the steps and timing for applying. The other three state commitments or entitlements, which makes them policy.

quiz.question: In the last six months a worker had 3 separate absence spells totalling 6 days. What is her Bradford factor?
quiz.explanation: S² × D = 3² × 6 = 9 × 6 = 54. 18 is S × D without squaring; 108 squares the days instead of the spells (6² × 3); 36 squares the days and ignores the spells.

quiz.question: Under ILO Convention 132 (1970), what is the minimum paid annual leave after a year of service?
options: Two weeks
Three working weeks
Four weeks
Six weeks
quiz.explanation: ILO Convention 132 sets at least three working weeks of paid leave for a year of service. Four weeks is the EU minimum under the Working Time Directive, and many countries go further. Always check the current local law.

quiz.question: A regional sales manager leaving the company claims the plant workers' collective agreement sets his notice period. Where should HR mainly look to settle his notice terms?
options: The plant workers' collective agreement, which covers everyone on the site
The minimum wage rules for his grade
The customer's code of conduct
His employment contract and the company policy for managers
quiz.explanation: A collective agreement covers the workers it was negotiated for, and worker-protection rules focus on workers. A manager's terms come mainly from his contract and the company's policy for managers.

quiz.question: A packer has been absent on three of the last five Mondays, each time with a phone message. What should the supervisor do first?
options: Issue a final written warning for habitual absence
Hold a return-to-work talk to understand why and note the pattern
Deduct an extra day's pay for each Monday missed, as a deterrent to others
Ignore it, since each absence was reported by phone
quiz.explanation: A supportive return-to-work talk finds causes and signals that patterns are noticed, before any formal step under a consistent trigger. Jumping to a final warning or extra deductions is unfair and may be unlawful.

quiz.question: What most strengthens a company's ability to apply a new attendance policy fairly on the shop floor?
options: Versions in the languages people read, supervisor training and signed acknowledgments
Publishing it on the intranet in English only, with an email to all staff
Approval by the board without consulting anyone
A strong opening statement from the CEO
quiz.explanation: People must be able to read, understand and confirm a policy before it can be fairly enforced. An English-only intranet page or board approval alone does not reach plant workers.

sessions.title: Employee Relations, Grievances and Fair Discipline
sessions.summary: Keep the peace on the shop floor by handling grievances quickly and fairly, running disciplinary cases that respect natural justice from show-cause notice to inquiry and decision, choosing proportionate penalties, and supporting the separate process that harassment laws require.
objectives: Tell grievances, disciplinary matters and harassment complaints apart and route each correctly
Apply the principles of natural justice to every disciplinary case
Draft a specific show-cause notice and run an impartial inquiry with a proper record
Choose proportionate, consistent penalties and tell termination apart from dismissal for misconduct
Explain the duties that the ILO's 2019 convention and national harassment laws place on employers

cards.title: Thirty missing cartons
cards.setting: Nairobi plant floor. 11 pm, night shift. The loading-bay CCTV screen is frozen on a grey van.

lines.text: Stage four. Forty-five days to the audit. Tonight the Hearing Room opens without warning.
Thirty cartons of milk powder gone. The camera shows Daniel from dispatch loading a private van. I told him on the floor: you're fired, get out.
Daniel says he was loading a sample consignment on his supervisor's instruction. Fired in front of everyone without a hearing? The night shift is ready to stop the line.
And there's something else. A packing-line operator just sent me a WhatsApp voice note. She says her shift supervisor keeps sending her messages at night that make her afraid to come in.
Two serious matters, two different processes, one angry shop floor. Get either wrong and we lose the people, the case, and probably the audit.
Your mission tonight: make sure both are handled fairly. What does fair actually require?

scenes.heading: Know the case
scenes.narration: A person accused of misconduct must be told exactly what they are accused of: what, when, where, which rule, and what evidence exists. A vague charge cannot be answered.

scenes.heading: Be heard
scenes.narration: They must get a fair chance to reply, to see the evidence against them, to question witnesses and to bring their own, usually with a co-worker or union representative beside them.

scenes.heading: An unbiased judge
scenes.narration: Nobody should judge a case they are part of. The witness, the complainant or the manager who already announced the verdict cannot run the inquiry.

scenes.heading: Decide on evidence
scenes.narration: Findings must rest on evidence recorded in the inquiry, not on rumours, past grudges or pressure from the top.

scenes.heading: Proportion and reasons
scenes.narration: The penalty must fit the proven misconduct and the person's record, be consistent with similar cases, be given in writing with reasons, and allow an appeal.

cards.title: A fair disciplinary process
cards.caption: Minor penalties may follow a show-cause notice and reply. Major penalties, such as dismissal, need a full inquiry first.

items.label: Incident and fact-finding
items.detail: Secure evidence: CCTV, gate passes, stock records, first statements

items.label: Suspension if needed
items.detail: Pending inquiry, to protect evidence or safety. Not a punishment

items.label: Show-cause notice
items.detail: Specific allegations, rule breached, evidence, time to reply in writing

items.label: Reply considered
items.detail: If accepted, close or caution; if not, proceed to inquiry

items.label: Impartial inquiry
items.detail: Hearing, witnesses, cross-questioning, representative present, signed minutes

items.label: Findings and decision
items.detail: Inquiry officer finds facts; a separate authority decides the penalty

items.label: Written order and appeal
items.detail: Reasons stated; route and deadline for appeal given

cards.title: Real case: the Post Office Horizon scandal (UK)
cards.body:
**What happened.** From around 2000, the UK Post Office relied on data from its Horizon computer system to accuse branch operators (subpostmasters) of cash shortfalls. Hundreds were prosecuted for theft or false accounting, and many more were made to repay money or lost their branches. Those who said the system was wrong were often told nobody else had problems.

**Outcome.** In 2019 the High Court found that Horizon had bugs, errors and defects that could cause false shortfalls. The Court of Appeal quashed dozens of convictions in 2021, a 2024 law quashed many more, and a public inquiry has examined how it happened.

**Lesson for HR operations:** system data is evidence, not a verdict. Let the accused see and challenge it, check whether others have the same problem, and never treat a printout as proof that ends the inquiry.

cards.question: Diego announced on the shop floor that Daniel is fired. Why does that make Diego unsuitable to conduct Daniel's inquiry?
options: Plant managers are never allowed to take part in disciplinary matters
He has not yet received inquiry-officer training from HR
The union must always choose the inquiry officer
He has already declared a verdict, so he cannot be an unbiased judge
cards.explanation: Natural justice requires an unbiased decision-maker. Having announced the outcome, Diego has prejudged the case. Managers can take part in discipline generally, and the union does not choose the inquiry officer.

cards.title: Grievance, discipline or harassment?
cards.prompt: Route each matter to the process it belongs in.

items.text: A worker says his night-shift allowance has not been paid for two months
An operator complains the canteen roster always gives her team the last slot
A storekeeper is seen on CCTV removing stock without a gate pass
A forklift driver is found asleep on duty for the third time
A machine operator refuses a lawful instruction from his supervisor and shouts abuse
A supervisor repeatedly sends a junior colleague unwelcome late-night messages
A manager suggests a promotion depends on an employee meeting him privately after hours

cards.title: Writing a show-cause notice that holds up
cards.body:
A show-cause notice (or charge sheet) is the foundation of the whole case. If it is vague, everything built on it can collapse.

**Include:**
- **Specific allegations:** what happened, date, time, place. *"On 14 October at about 10:40 pm you loaded 30 cartons of milk powder into a private van without a gate pass."*
- **The rule or misconduct** it may amount to, such as theft or dishonesty under the disciplinary code, the misconduct list in law, or a named policy.
- **The evidence** relied on, and how the employee can see it.
- **Time to reply in writing**, as policy states (often several working days).
- **What happens next** if there is no reply or it is not satisfactory.
- **Suspension status**, if suspended, and the pay rules that apply.

**Avoid:** "your conduct has been unsatisfactory", conclusions ("you stole") before the inquiry, and bundling unrelated old complaints.

cards.title: Termination versus dismissal for misconduct
cards.caption: Mixing these up is one of the most common reasons an employer loses at a labour court or employment tribunal.

items.label: Reason
items.left: Redundancy, closure, end of contract, other non-fault grounds
items.right: Proven misconduct such as theft or insubordination

items.label: Process
items.left: Notice or pay in lieu as law and contract require
items.right: Charge, reply, inquiry, written findings

items.label: Written order
items.right: States the proven charges and reasons for penalty

items.label: Stigma
items.right: Recorded as misconduct

items.label: Exit dues
items.left: Notice, gratuity and other benefits per law and policy
items.right: Dues per law and policy; take advice before withholding anything

cards.title: The night shift waits
cards.setting: Plant HR office, 11:40 pm. Through the window you can see the night shift gathered by the canteen, machines idle.

lines.text: Give me something to tell them. Either Daniel gets a fair hearing or nobody touches a machine till morning.
I'm not taking back my words in front of the whole shift. A thief is a thief.
The CCTV shows loading. It doesn't show who authorised it. Daniel's supervisor hasn't been asked anything yet.
Diego, nobody is calling him innocent or guilty yet. That is exactly the point. What do we put in writing tonight?

cards.title: Undoing an on-the-spot firing
cards.situation: Daniel was told on the floor that he is fired. There is CCTV of loading but no record of who authorised it. The night shift has stopped work, and Samuel wants an answer now.

choices.text: Issue a dismissal letter tonight attaching the CCTV clip, since the evidence is clear
choices.outcome: The CCTV shows loading, not theft or authority. A dismissal without charge, reply or inquiry is likely to be overturned, and the shift sees management deciding first and asking later.

choices.text: Let Daniel return to his normal duties while HR asks around informally over the next few weeks
choices.outcome: It calms the floor, and avoids prejudging him. But with no formal process the case drifts, the dispatch area and records stay open to him, and no one can act on what is found.

choices.text: Ask Samuel to persuade Daniel to resign quietly so nobody loses face
choices.outcome: A pressured resignation can be challenged as a forced dismissal, and the real question of who took the cartons is never answered.

choices.text: Confirm in writing that no dismissal has been made, suspend Daniel pending inquiry, issue a specific show-cause notice, and name an independent inquiry officer; tell Samuel the steps
choices.outcome: The line restarts within the hour. Daniel's rights are protected, the evidence is safe, and the case can now end in any outcome the facts support, including dismissal if theft is proved.

cards.title: Handling an individual grievance
cards.prompt: Put the stages of a fair grievance procedure in order.
steps: Worker raises the issue informally with the immediate supervisor (or the next level if the supervisor is involved)
If unresolved, the worker submits a written grievance to HR
HR acknowledges it in writing and investigates the facts
A meeting is held where the worker explains, with a representative if wanted
A written decision with reasons is given within the policy's time limit
The worker may appeal to a higher authority, and beyond that to the statutory forum

cards.title: Running the inquiry
cards.body:
- **Inquiry officer:** independent of the incident, senior enough, trained. Never the complainant, a witness or a manager who has prejudged.
- **Notice of hearing:** date, place, right to bring a co-worker or union representative.
- **Evidence in the open:** management witnesses speak in the employee's presence; the employee may cross-question them and call their own.
- **Documents:** the employee may see what is relied on, such as CCTV, gate registers and stock records.
- **Minutes:** recorded at each sitting and signed by those present. The local language is fine; accuracy matters more.
- **Report:** a finding on each charge, with reasons drawn from the evidence. The inquiry officer recommends; the competent authority decides.
- **Parallel police case:** an internal inquiry can usually proceed, because it asks a different question to a lower standard of proof. Take legal advice.
- **Time:** move briskly. Long suspensions are unfair and costly.

cards.title: Spot the breach
cards.prompt: Match each flawed practice to the principle it breaks.

pairs.right: Know the case: allegations must be specific enough to answer

pairs.left: Witnesses interviewed privately and never produced
pairs.right: Right to be heard, including testing the evidence

pairs.left: The complainant's own manager runs the inquiry
pairs.right: An unbiased decision-maker

pairs.left: Dismissed for a first late arrival of ten minutes
pairs.right: Proportionality of penalty

pairs.left: Two workers, same proven offence, same record: one dismissed, one warned
